title: Fearless, changeless
hookLine: the Jaap keeps returning to fearlessness, a quality at the heart of the Khalsa ideal
last: EK ACHHARI — AJAI, ALAI, ABHAI, ABAI.

lines: A WORD SAID AGAINST THE WEIGHT.
cards: Fear has a body. A tight chest before the phone call. Cold hands before the exam results open.
A stomach that drops when the boss says, got a minute? Plenty of people carry a few fears around like stones in a pocket: money, health, being left, being found out.
The weight gets so familiar they forget it's there, until something makes them reach in and touch one. Jaap Sahib, recited every morning, keeps saying one word against that weight.

teach.b: The word is abhai. Bhai is fear; a is without. Fearless.

It's in the one-letter meter, and it returns again and again in other stanzas beside its partners: unconquerable, unchanging, unborn. Of all the qualities Jaap praises, fearlessness is one it simply won't let go of.
Sikhs met the idea long before Jaap.
The Mool Mantar, at the very start of the Guru Granth Sahib, calls the One nirbhau, without fear, and nirvair, without hatred, side by side. Guru Nanak's opening and the Tenth Guru's praise agree.
Then comes the turn that matters for daily life: Sikhs don't praise fearlessness only as something God has. They hope to grow toward it.
The ninth Guru, Guru Tegh Bahadur, the Tenth Guru's father, wrote that the wise person is the one who frightens no one, and fears no one. Both halves: not a bully, and not a coward.
Sikhs remember him living it; tradition tells of him going to Delhi and to his execution rather than abandon the freedom of others to practice their faith.

teach.h: FRIGHTEN NO ONE, FEAR NO ONE.
teach.b: Fearlessness sits at the heart of the Khalsa ideal his son founded: a people meant to stand up without fear and without hate, and never to put fear into the innocent.
As Sikh teachers often put it, people grow a little like what they praise every morning.
Saying abhai doesn't make fear vanish. The hope is that fear stops being the one deciding.

how: Sikhs say nirbhau, without fear, every day in the Mool Mantar and abhai many times in Jaap Sahib, and fearlessness without hatred is central to the Khalsa ideal.

o: without hatred toward anyone at all
never feeling any pain or sorrow

p: without fear, in the Mool Mantar
fear no one, frighten no one

s: fearlessness appears only once in Jaap
abhai keeps coming back, beside unconquerable, unchanging and unborn.
the Mool Mantar pairs fearless with without hatred
Guru Tegh Bahadur praised those who make others afraid
he called wise the one who frightens no one and fears no one.

games.q: Guru Tegh Bahadur describes the wise person in two halves. which pair is it?
o: fears no one, and frightens no one.
fears nothing, and cares about nothing.
games.why: not a bully and not a coward: the wise one neither gives fear nor takes it (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1427).

practice: Pick up one stone from the pocket and name it, silently and plainly: I'm afraid of this. Notice where it sits in your body, chest, stomach, shoulders, jaw, and breathe into that place without trying to make the fear leave.
If you like, say abhai on the out-breath a few times, not to argue with the fear, just to remind it who else is here.

wordCard.voice: Abhai. Without fear: the quality Jaap keeps returning to, echoing nirbhau in the Mool Mantar.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: abhai, without fear, from bhai, fear; compare nirbhau in the Mool Mantar.

carryVoice: Your line: fearless like him. Frighten no one, and fear no one. Day three hundred fifty-two, done.

sources.ref: Jaap Sahib: abhai (ek achhari and other stanzas)
Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1 (Mool Mantar): nirbhau, nirvair
Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1427 (salok, Guru Tegh Bahadur): frightens no one, fears no one
